title: Simo B2 First level listening - source transcripts

segments.text: I was offered the team-leader position in April, which would have meant a higher salary and a title I could put on my CV. People assumed I turned it down because I was nervous about managing staff. The truth was simpler: the job required a fixed late shift three evenings a week. My current hours are flexible enough for me to collect my daughter from school, and for the time being that matters more than a promotion.

When the council announced cycle lanes on the high street, I thought they'd be a waste of money. Six months later, the number of people cycling to work has clearly increased, and the traffic hasn't become as terrible as opponents predicted. That said, the junction near the library is still genuinely dangerous. I'd support extending the scheme, provided they sort out that crossing first.

The menu looked fairly ordinary at first, and the waiter seemed in a terrible hurry to take our order. Yet the dishes were far more imaginative than we'd expected, particularly the roasted vegetables with lemon. We would have stayed for dessert, but the staff started clearing the neighbouring tables while people were still eating. I wouldn't complain about the cooking; it's the way the restaurant treats its customers that needs attention.

The plane being late wasn't the real issue. Delays happen, and I can understand that when there's bad weather. What annoyed me was that the screens showed the original departure time long after the staff had told some passengers a different one. We ended up walking between gates with no idea which information to trust. A clear announcement would have made the whole experience much less stressful.

People imagine that you need expert knowledge to help with our community garden, but that's really not the case. The professional gardener decides what to plant, while volunteers do everything from watering seedlings to painting old benches. We actually value people who turn up regularly more than people who arrive with impressive qualifications. Even an hour every fortnight makes a real difference.
I was nearly ready to leave at the interval. The opening scenes seemed to drag, and I couldn't understand why the director had moved the action to the present day.
I noticed you were getting restless, but the second half brought everything together. The final scene was incredibly moving.
Exactly. It made me reconsider those strange choices at the beginning. I still wouldn't call the production perfect, but I enjoyed it far more than I expected to after the first act.
Recorded lectures are useful when I'm revising because I can stop and replay the complicated bits.
True, but it isn't the same as being in the room. You miss the unexpected questions that make a teacher explain something differently.
I agree. That's why I'd hate a course that was entirely prerecorded. I like being able to review lessons later, but I still want regular sessions where I can discuss ideas with other students.

I've been experimenting with software that turns quick sketches into finished designs. Some people say this will make designers unnecessary; others believe every design should be produced by hand. Neither argument convinces me. The software can speed up routine tasks, but it can't decide which idea is worth developing. We still need people who are curious, critical and willing to make mistakes.

Good afternoon. My name's Hannah Reed, and for the last four years I've been helping restore an area of coastal wetland called Kingmere Marsh. People are sometimes surprised to discover that I didn't study environmental science. I trained as a graphic designer, and I spent nearly a decade working on advertising campaigns before I took part in a weekend conservation project. One afternoon outdoors completely changed the direction of my career.

When I arrived at Kingmere, the ground looked rather unpromising: long stretches of dry grass, an abandoned track and very little open water. What first helped us understand the scale of the problem wasn't an expensive new machine. We compared satellite photographs taken over twenty years, which showed us where the sea had once reached inland. Those pictures became the basis of our restoration plan.

Not everybody welcomed the idea. Some residents feared that increased flooding would damage their houses. Others worried that the project might attract too many visitors. But the complaint we heard most frequently at public meetings was about the smell people expected from the wetland. In fact, healthy marshes rarely smell unpleasant, and explaining that became an important part of our work.

Our first volunteer weekend was memorable for the wrong reasons. We had ordered ordinary gardening gloves and strong jackets, but we forgot that the ground would be extremely muddy. Several people went home with ruined trainers. The following week we bought rubber boots for everyone, and we've insisted on wearing them ever since.

One of the most exciting moments came the next spring when a pair of terns, small seabirds with sharp wings, began nesting in an area we had recently restored. We had expected ducks to return first, so seeing the terns was a wonderful surprise. We made sure volunteers kept their distance, especially while the birds were feeding their young.

Visitors can now explore part of the site, although access is deliberately restricted to protect the wildlife. Rather than building a traditional road, we've installed a raised walkway across the wettest section. It allows people to see the marsh without damaging plants. We did consider using stepping stones, but those would have been unsafe after heavy rain.

Funding has been another challenge. A national charity helped us with specialist advice, and the council provided permissions, but most of the money for the walkway and signs actually came from local businesses. Several shop owners said a healthier coastline would benefit the whole town.

Research matters just as much as practical work. Every month, university students visit the marsh to measure the water level and record which insects have returned. Their findings are shared with our volunteers. Professional researchers occasionally join them, but it's the students who collect most of the regular data.

We had planned a community celebration in September last year. Unfortunately, strong winds meant that the outdoor activities weren't safe, so the event was postponed until October. The extra few weeks turned out to be helpful, because we could finish the visitor information boards.

Looking ahead, people have suggested adding a small café or an indoor exhibition. Both ideas have supporters. Our priority, however, is an observation tower at the northern edge of the marsh. It would help visitors watch birds without disturbing them. We hope to begin construction next summer. If you would like to volunteer, look at our website for details. Thank you very much for listening.

I enrolled in a pottery course because I'd always liked making things with my hands. I imagined I'd be turning out beautiful bowls within a month. Instead, I was constantly rushing from the office, and I rarely touched the clay between lessons. The tutor was excellent, and the other students were supportive, so that wasn't the problem. Looking back, I should have protected a couple of evenings each week to repeat what we'd learnt. I might have improved much faster.

I took an evening course in photography purely for pleasure. My colleagues teased me about carrying a camera everywhere. But when our company needed pictures of a product launch, the marketing team asked me to help, and I ended up producing images that went straight onto our website. It was quite a surprise, because I hadn't thought my hobby had anything to do with my day job. Now I even photograph some of our events.

When I started learning Italian, I was determined to master grammar and pronunciation. I chose a group class instead of studying alone because it was cheaper. What I hadn't anticipated was how much fun I'd have meeting people with different backgrounds. We still go for coffee together even though the course ended months ago. My vocabulary could certainly be better, but those friendships have probably been the best thing to come out of it.

For years I avoided swimming in deep water. I could manage a few lengths in a shallow pool, but as soon as I couldn't touch the bottom I panicked. My instructor didn't push me straight into the deep end. We worked gradually on breathing and floating, and I began to trust myself. I wouldn't say I'm ready to swim across a lake, but now I can enjoy a normal swimming pool without feeling frightened.

I bought a second-hand guitar because I couldn't justify spending a fortune on an instrument I might abandon. At first I envied people with shiny new models, but my teacher showed me how much you can do with a basic guitar if you practise carefully. A musician friend offered to lend me a professional one. I tried it, of course, but it didn't suddenly make me play better. That was an important lesson.

Welcome to Inside the City. This week I'm talking to sound artist Daniel Foster, who records everyday sounds in towns and cities. Daniel, you originally worked in theatre. Why did you become interested in field recording?

I enjoyed theatre and still do, so it wasn't an attempt to escape a profession I disliked. It began when I was walking home one evening and noticed the extraordinary rhythms made by trains crossing a bridge. I'd passed that bridge hundreds of times without really hearing it. I started wondering what else we fail to notice in familiar places. That curiosity, rather than a plan to change careers, was the beginning.
Your first major project involved travelling to twelve different cities. How was it funded?

I applied for an arts grant and was lucky enough to receive one, but it only covered transport and accommodation. I'd imagined I would need to buy expensive microphones, but there was no money left for that. Fortunately a local radio station lent me some equipment. The trip itself cost exactly what I'd budgeted, although editing the recordings took far longer than expected.
Was it difficult to capture clear sounds outdoors?

Technically, yes: wind, traffic and people talking can ruin a recording. But I learnt to solve most of those problems quite quickly. The much harder task was deciding which sounds were actually interesting. You can record hundreds of hours of material and still have very little worth using. I had to learn to be selective instead of collecting absolutely everything.
You also worked with residents in each city. Did they change your approach?

Completely. I arrived with a list of what I considered typical urban sounds: buses, markets, construction sites. Then residents took me to quiet courtyards, neighbourhood football pitches and even a staircase where people could hear their own footsteps echo. These places rarely appeared in tourist guides, yet they carried powerful memories for the people who lived there. I realised my original idea of a city's identity was rather narrow.
A number of your recordings are free to listen to online. What do you hope people will get from them?

Some listeners use them to remember places they've lived, which I find moving. Others enjoy them as a kind of background music. Both are welcome, but the main thing I want is for someone to remove their headphones afterwards and pay closer attention to what's happening around them. I'm not trying to produce a perfect historical archive of every sound.
I understand you've begun using older recording machines. Why?

Not because I think the sound quality is superior. Modern digital equipment is astonishing. With an old machine, though, you can only record for a limited time before changing the tape. That restriction forces me to stop, listen and decide what matters. It has made me much more patient and deliberate, which is especially valuable when I'm working alone.
Finally, what's next for you?

People assume I'll visit even bigger and noisier cities, but next summer I'm working in three small rural villages. I want to challenge the assumption that quiet places are somehow empty of interesting sounds. They have their own complex rhythms if you're prepared to listen. I hope the experience will make me question a few more of my habits.
